[{:db/id 17592186179778 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/id #uuid "e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-124289" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=u-v-1,\,y=3v-2u-6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+y+9,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-1 \\ 3v-2u-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ -2u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+1 \\ y+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6) \\ 2\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3x+y+9 \\ 2x+y+8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=3x+y+9,\,v=2x+y+8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+2+8=13.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-20065c9e-4427-527a-a708-a46b3d2f2065"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the quadrilateral under the action of $T$ is a line segment." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "q-124289"] ["question-e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=u-v-1,\,y=3v-2u-6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+y+9,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$"] ["question-e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-1 \\ 3v-2u-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ -2u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+1 \\ y+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6) \\ 2\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3x+y+9 \\ 2x+y+8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=3x+y+9,\,v=2x+y+8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+2+8=13.
$$"] ["question-e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-20065c9e-4427-527a-a708-a46b3d2f2065" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the quadrilateral under the action of $T$ is a line segment."] ["question-353e50fd-8521-51a5-ae98-273dc887e6d8" :question/difficulty 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ -1 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 8-9\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}5 & -9 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}5 & -9 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=\frac{5}{4}+(-\frac{9}{4})+2=1.

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7+(-4)x-y,\,v=3x+y+(-5).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

What would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3)-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} {:db/id 17592186180096 :question/id #uuid "2a5baf7e-c7c5-5ee4-b2ff-f2b8dad11ff2" [{:db/id 17592186180565 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180763 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}$$

This equation gives us a method of computing the inverse of an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:

*An affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\det(A) \neq 0.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf99caa7-1e47-5fea-87ac-9b91151af127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7697 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35dfb0c0-efab-5193-92eb-6eb22cc2af9f" :step/math-academy-id 44660 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180566}} {:db/id 17592186180566 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179776 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179437 :question/id #uuid "f9d3291b-b95b-536b-93ec-9815f7f554d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12428"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e39ae7fc-ff0a-5b97-8e13-1f15b12a07e5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049018} {:db/id 17592186049554}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179998} {:db/id 17592186179999} {:db/id 17592186259624} {:db/id 17592186259626} {:db/id 17592186259627} {:db/id 17592186259629} {:db/id 17592186378496} {:db/id 17592186378503} {:db/id 17592186378510}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "30275202-8cd8-51e0-a9e1-92aa287dbe42" :step/math-academy-id 44661 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180567}} {:db/id 17592186180567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ expressed in matrix form as

$$\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{\mathbf x} = \underbrace{[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{\mathbf b}.$$

We wish to determine whether $\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist.

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned} \right| = 1\cdot (-2) - (-3) \cdot 1 = 1 \neq 0.$$

Since $\det(A) \neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible.

To compute the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ we will use the formula we derived earlier:

$$\mathbf{u} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})$$

We start by calculating the inverse of $A{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}$$

:tutorial/content "Consider the square in the $uv$-plane shown below.

![](images/a8/a8cc0923da86a1a1ac6b666893397263ef3865448080500caa6f17510547d901.png)

We wish to explore the image of this square under an affine transformation $$\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},$$ where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors.

Similar to linear transformations, there are three possibilities depending on the value of $\det(A)$.

- $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular ($\det(A)\neq 0$). In this case, our square is mapped to a parallelogram.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] + [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane, we get the following parallelogram:

![](images/36/36da067393fa53f4296373d65e3c6177a54d1a901824188687b4a74ea171afdf.png)
- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ has at least one nonzero entry. In this case, our square is mapped to a line segment.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}] \cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] + [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following line segment:

![](images/5e/5e5481e5b2f2218a6097020e260dc991cde05574372c724aa07527458257d94c.png)
- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ is the zero matrix. In this case, our square is mapped to a point on the plane.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] + [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following point.

![](images/00/0072c5e06674f79f82e771744fda217e6558830f7a6e4ab387aa9dbf4dda09bc.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "375d6591-08dd-5dbf-b36a-28013839a28b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7706 :tutorial/title "Image Types Formed by Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "5ec4662b-6870-532f-83f9-f7a9cbe5504e" :step/math-academy-id 44705 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180576}} {:db/id 17592186180576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180768 :tutorial/content "In general, if we consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the mapping

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, then we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases: 

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane (namely, the point with position vector $\mathbf b$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "560907bc-354a-5693-a8df-e6824454755d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7710 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Image Types"} :step/id #uuid "d71cf118-7383-5aea-a47c-8359fc7dffe4" :step/math-academy-id 44723 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180574}}] :activity/title "The Inverse of an Affine Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179866} {:db/id 17592186180565 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180763 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}$$
